questions.q: In the lesson's simplified equation of exchange, what does V represent?
options: The total vesting duration of team allocations
Velocity -- how many times, on average, a token changes hands per year
questions.explain: V is velocity: how frequently a token turns over in transactions per year.

questions.q: A protocol processes $50,000,000/year in transaction volume. At velocity V=2 vs. V=20, what happens to the token's required market value?
options: It stays exactly the same regardless of velocity
Velocity has no mathematical relationship to required token value in this model
It drops from $25,000,000 (V=2) to $2,500,000 (V=20) -- higher velocity needs less token value to support the same usage
questions.explain: Token_value_needed = (P x Q) / V. Dividing the same $50,000,000 by a larger V produces a smaller required token value.

questions.q: Why is high token velocity generally a problem for a utility token's price?
options: A token that's bought, used, and immediately sold supports the same economic activity with much less market value backing it
High velocity always causes a protocol to be hacked
High velocity guarantees the token's price will rise
Velocity has no effect on price, only on gas fees
questions.explain: Higher velocity means less token market value is needed to support the same transaction volume, which works against price for a purely pass-through utility token.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as an inflow that increases circulating supply, per this lesson's model?
questions.explain: Vesting unlocks are an inflow (they add previously-locked tokens to circulating supply); burns and new lockups are outflows.
